Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- As the first president-elect with a Facebook page and a YouTube channel, Barack Obama is poised to use the Internet to communicate directly with Americans in a way unknown to previous presidents. Since the election, President-elect Barack Obama has posted weekly video addresses on YouTube. Judging by Obama's savvy use of social-networking sites during his campaign and the interactive nature of his transition team's Web site, Americans can expect a president who bypasses the traditional media's filters while reaching out to citizens for input, observers say. "The rebooting of our democracy has begun," said Andrew Rasiej, founder of Personal Democracy Forum and the techPresident blog. "[Obama] has the potential to transform the relationship between the American public and their democracy." During the presidential race, Obama's campaign won praise for its innovative use of social-networking sites, including Facebook, MySpace and MyBarackObama.com, to announce events, rally volunteers and raise money. Facebook has more than 150 million active users, and the average user has 100 friends on the site, according to the company. iReport.com: Your chance to ask President-elect Obama a question . Obama has more than 1 million MySpace "friends" and more than 3.7 million "supporters" on his official Facebook page -- some 700,000 more than when he was elected in November. His campaign also has a database of almost 13 million supporters and their e-mail addresses. Transition officials hope to transform Obama's vast Web operation and electronic list of supporters into a 21st-century tool to help accomplish his goals as president. They even have a name for this ambitious effort: Obama 2.0. "Obama has invented an alternative media model," said CNN senior political analyst Bill Schneider. "In the old model, the president talks to the people on television [and] the people talk back in polls. In the new model, communication is online, and two-way." Facebook, MySpace, YouTube and Twitter didn't exist when George W. Bush took office eight years ago. But since last November's election, Obama has wasted no time embracing these online communication portals. In recent weeks he has taped weekly video addresses and posted them to YouTube, where most have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times. Obama's staffers also have stopped posting information to social-networking sites since the election, preferring to reach out to constituents through YouTube and Change.gov, the official site of the president-elect's transition team. Visitors to Change.gov can read a frequently updated blog, post their ideas on issues facing the country, and rate others' ideas. Top-rated ideas will be gathered into a briefing book and given to Obama after he takes office. "They want information going not just from them to the voters, but from the voters back to them," Democratic strategist Steve McMahon said Wednesday on CNN's "The Situation Room." "Thirteen million people pushing a button, sending an e-mail to their elected representatives, making a phone call, taking action, is a powerful, powerful lobbying tool." "It's a very smart use of the Internet, to get people to offer ideas," said David All, a Republican Internet strategist. All hopes that Obama and his staff take a similar approach to WhiteHouse.gov, the president's official Web site. The current WhiteHouse.gov site, operated by the Bush administration, contains few interactive features. A statement on the president-elect's transition site says that Obama hopes to "use cutting-edge technologies to create a new level of transparency, accountability, and participation for America's citizens." It's fitting, then, that Obama's inauguration next week could be one of the most watched video events in Internet history. Rasiej expects that hordes of users will be watching online when Obama takes the oath of office, visiting WhiteHouse.gov and refreshing their browsers to capture the moment the site switches to proclaim Obama, not George W. Bush, as president. As president, Obama will likely not just rely on WhiteHouse.gov but use multiple Internet sites and technological tools to build grass-roots support for his agenda, observers say. "[Obama] is using the tools that are available to him today," All told CNN. "The next president will be using some of the same tools, and also some tools that haven't been invented yet."

Barack Obama’s transition team entered the post-election period with an ambitious goal: to change not only the policies of the federal government, but also the way the presidency communicated with the public. After a campaign that had made unprecedented use of the internet, social networking platforms, online video, text messaging and email organizing, Obama’s advisers sought to bring many of those same tools into the work of governing.

The idea was to move beyond the traditional model in which presidents relied heavily on press conferences, televised speeches and news organizations to deliver their message. Instead, the incoming administration hoped to speak directly to citizens through social networks, YouTube addresses, large email lists and interactive websites. These tools could allow the White House to explain its priorities, respond quickly to events, invite public input and mobilize supporters around key issues.

During the campaign, Obama’s online operation had helped build a vast community of volunteers, donors and supporters. Millions of people received campaign updates by email or text message, watched speeches online, shared videos with friends and used digital tools to organize local events. The transition team wanted to preserve that network and adapt it for a new purpose: encouraging citizens to stay involved after Election Day.

One early example was the use of weekly video addresses posted online, making presidential communication available on demand rather than only through scheduled television broadcasts. Another was the creation of websites where Americans could learn about the transition, submit questions, offer ideas and track policy proposals. These efforts suggested a more open and participatory approach, one in which citizens were not simply passive recipients of information but potential contributors to the governing process.

Observers described this emerging strategy as “Obama 2.0,” a reference to the interactive culture of Web 2.0. Supporters argued that it could create a more direct and two-way relationship between the public and the presidency. Instead of filtering every message through newspapers or television networks, the administration could communicate with Americans instantly and personally. At the same time, citizens could respond, organize and make their concerns visible in new ways.

The potential consequences for democracy were significant. If successful, this model could make government feel more accessible and encourage broader civic participation, especially among younger Americans already accustomed to online communication. It could also increase transparency by giving people more information about decisions, appointments and policy debates.

However, the approach also raised questions. Direct communication from the White House could reduce the role of traditional journalists, whose job includes questioning official claims and providing independent analysis. Online participation might also favor those with reliable internet access and strong digital skills, leaving some citizens less represented. In addition, a large online supporter network could be used not only to inform the public but also to pressure lawmakers and shape political debate.

Even with these concerns, Obama’s digital strategy marked an important moment in the evolution of presidential communication. It reflected a broader shift in American politics, as campaigns and governments began to recognize that citizens increasingly expected to interact, comment, share and participate online. The “Obama 2.0” model suggested that the relationship between Americans and their government might become more immediate, more interactive and potentially more democratic than in the past.

**Obama turns to Internet to speak directly to Americans before taking office**

*WASHINGTON* — President-elect Barack Obama is not waiting until Inauguration Day to begin reshaping how the White House communicates with the public.

In the weeks after his historic election, Obama and his transition team have leaned heavily on the Internet — from YouTube addresses to a new transition Web site, Change.gov — to speak directly to Americans, gather ideas and keep millions of supporters engaged.

The strategy reflects a continuation of the digital operation that helped power Obama’s campaign, which used e-mail, text messaging, social networking sites and online fundraising to build a national grassroots network.

Now, the challenge is turning that campaign machinery into a tool for governing.

Obama’s transition team has posted weekly video addresses online, reviving the traditional presidential radio address for the YouTube era. The videos allow Obama to outline his priorities — including the economy, health care and energy — without relying solely on television networks or newspapers to deliver his message.

The president-elect has also used Change.gov as a central hub for information about the transition. The site has featured policy proposals, announcements about Cabinet appointments and opportunities for Americans to submit questions or share personal stories about the issues facing the country.

For supporters who spent months organizing house parties, making phone calls and donating small amounts online, the Web outreach is a sign that the Obama team intends to keep them involved.

During the campaign, Obama’s online operation became one of the most sophisticated in American politics. His team built a vast database of supporters, raised hundreds of millions of dollars through the Internet and used social media platforms such as Facebook and MySpace to spread messages quickly.

The campaign also made extensive use of YouTube, posting speeches, advertisements and behind-the-scenes clips that could be watched and shared at any time. One of the advantages was cost: online videos could reach millions of viewers without the expense of buying television time.

Political analysts say Obama’s use of digital tools helped him connect with younger voters and gave supporters a sense of personal involvement in the campaign.

But governing online could prove more complicated than campaigning online.

As president, Obama will face legal, security and archival rules that do not apply to a campaign. Communications from the White House may be subject to federal record-keeping requirements. There are also concerns about how interactive a government Web site can be while protecting privacy and maintaining security.

Still, Obama advisers have made clear that they see the Internet as a central part of the incoming administration’s communications strategy.

The approach could mark a significant shift from past presidencies, where public communication was dominated by televised speeches, press briefings and carefully staged events. Obama’s team appears determined to add a more direct digital channel — one that allows the president to bypass traditional filters and speak to Americans on their computers and phones.

The effort also carries political benefits. By keeping supporters connected, Obama may be able to mobilize public backing for major legislation once he takes office, including an economic recovery package.

For now, the president-elect’s online presence offers a preview of how he may govern: with an emphasis on speed, accessibility and direct communication.

Obama campaigned on a promise of change. Before even entering the White House, he is already changing the way a president-elect talks to the country.

**CNN — 2009**

**Obama Team Turns to Social Media to Build a More Interactive Presidency**

As President-elect Barack Obama prepares to take office, his campaign’s groundbreaking use of the Internet is moving from election strategy to governing strategy.

After relying heavily on online organizing during the 2008 campaign, Obama’s transition team is now using sites such as **Facebook, MySpace, YouTube, Twitter and Change.gov** to keep supporters engaged — and to invite Americans to take part in the political process in ways that were not possible in previous administrations.

Throughout the campaign, Obama’s team used social networking tools to raise money, recruit volunteers and spread messages quickly. Supporters received updates online, shared videos with friends and organized local events through campaign platforms and popular social media sites.

Now, those same tools are being adapted for the transition to the White House.

At the center of that effort is **Change.gov**, the official transition website. The site features policy information, announcements, videos and opportunities for citizens to submit ideas and comments. The transition team has described it as part of an effort to make government more open and accessible.

Obama has also used **YouTube** to deliver weekly video addresses — a modern version of the traditional presidential radio address. Instead of speaking only over the airwaves, Obama’s messages can be watched, embedded and shared online by millions of viewers.

On **Facebook** and **MySpace**, Obama’s pages continue to serve as gathering places for supporters. During the campaign, Obama built one of the largest online political followings in American history. His team is now trying to convert that campaign community into a governing community.

**Twitter**, still a relatively new platform, is also part of the communications mix. Short updates allow Obama’s team to distribute news quickly and direct users to longer statements, videos and policy materials.

The approach reflects a broader shift in American politics. Rather than relying solely on television speeches, press conferences and newspaper coverage, the incoming administration is experimenting with direct communication — reaching citizens where they already spend time online.

Political observers say the strategy could change expectations for the presidency. Voters who became accustomed to instant updates and online participation during the campaign may now expect the same kind of access from the White House.

But the move also presents challenges. Governing is different from campaigning, and online enthusiasm may be difficult to sustain once the administration faces contentious policy decisions. There are also questions about how much influence citizen comments and online forums will actually have on decision-making.

Still, Obama’s digital strategy marks a significant moment in presidential communication. From **YouTube addresses** to **Change.gov forums**, the incoming administration is signaling that the Internet will be more than a campaign tool — it will be part of how the next president tries to govern.

For a generation raised on social networks and online video, the Obama team is betting that democracy can become more interactive — one post, video and status update at a time.

---

# “Obama 2.0”: How a Digital Presidency Could Redefine Communication

**WASHINGTON** — Barack Obama’s rise to the presidency was powered not only by speeches, rallies and television ads, but by a digital machine unlike anything American politics had seen before. Now, as he prepares to govern, the central question is whether the tools that helped him win the White House can also help him run it.

Call it **Obama 2.0**: a presidency shaped by social networking, online organizing and direct digital communication with citizens.

During the campaign, Obama’s team built a sprawling online network of supporters through email, text messaging, social media and its own organizing platform, My.BarackObama.com. Millions of people donated small amounts, shared campaign videos, organized neighborhood events and received rapid updates directly from the campaign. The strategy helped Obama bypass traditional political gatekeepers and speak directly to voters.

The challenge now is whether that campaign model can be transformed into a governing model.

## From campaign followers to citizen participants

Obama enters office with an enormous digital audience — not just passive supporters, but people who were encouraged to see themselves as participants in a movement. That creates both an opportunity and a risk.

On one hand, the incoming administration could use the internet to explain policy proposals, rally support for legislation and invite public feedback. Online town halls, streaming video addresses, policy forums and digital petitions could give citizens new ways to interact with the White House.

On the other hand, governing is more complicated than campaigning. A campaign can ask supporters to donate, volunteer or vote. A president must make compromises, negotiate with Congress, manage crises and disappoint segments of his own coalition.

The same online army that helped amplify Obama’s message could also pressure him when his decisions fall short of expectations.

## A direct line around the press

Presidents have always tried to master the dominant communications technology of their era. Franklin Roosevelt used radio fireside chats to speak directly into American homes. John F. Kennedy excelled on television. Ronald Reagan understood the power of stagecraft and televised messaging. Obama may become the first truly internet-native president.

That could shift the relationship between the White House, the news media and the public.

Instead of relying primarily on press conferences or evening news coverage, the Obama administration could release videos, blog posts, emails and social media updates on its own terms. A presidential message posted online can be watched, shared and discussed instantly. Supporters can spread it through their own networks before traditional news organizations have fully framed the story.

This does not mean the press becomes irrelevant. Reporters will still investigate, challenge and interpret presidential claims. But the White House may gain more power to set the initial narrative — especially among younger voters accustomed to receiving news through digital platforms.

## Transparency or managed participation?

Obama has promised a more open and transparent government, and technology could help deliver on that pledge. The administration could post government data online, publish policy discussions, invite public comment and make federal agencies more accessible.

But digital participation also raises questions. Will online input meaningfully shape policy, or will it function mainly as political branding? Will the administration welcome criticism from its online community, or use digital tools mostly to mobilize support for decisions already made?

There is also the issue of scale. Millions of comments, suggestions and complaints cannot easily be translated into coherent policy. Online participation can democratize access, but it can also privilege those with the time, technology and motivation to engage.

## The permanent campaign goes digital

If Obama continues to use campaign-style networking from the White House, it could intensify what political scientists call the “permanent campaign” — the idea that presidents keep organizing public support long after Election Day.

For major fights over health care, energy, the economy or foreign policy, Obama could call on his digital supporters to contact lawmakers, attend events and push messages through social networks. That would give the White House a powerful tool to pressure Congress.

But it could also deepen partisan divisions if presidential communication becomes less about persuasion across the aisle and more about mobilizing loyal supporters.

## A new expectation for future presidents

Whatever the outcome, Obama’s digital strategy is likely to change what Americans expect from future presidents. Citizens may come to expect immediate updates, online access, interactive forums and a sense of direct connection to the White House.

The presidency has always been partly about communication. What may be changing is the direction of that communication. Instead of a one-way broadcast from president to public, Obama’s team has suggested a more networked model — one in which citizens talk back, organize themselves and become part of the political process between elections.

Whether that leads to a more engaged democracy or simply a more sophisticated form of message control will depend on how the tools are used.

For now, Obama’s victory has shown that social networking can help win a presidential campaign. The next test is whether it can help transform the presidency itself.

# Barack Obama and the Rise of the First Internet-Savvy President

When Barack Obama won the presidency in 2008, he did more than break a historic racial barrier. He also marked a turning point in the relationship between American politics and the Internet. Obama entered the White House as the first truly Internet-savvy president, having built a campaign that treated social media, online video, email lists, and interactive websites not as novelties, but as central tools of political organizing.

From his highly active Facebook presence to weekly YouTube addresses and the launch of Change.gov during the presidential transition, Obama’s team helped redefine how a president could communicate with voters in the digital age.

“Obama’s campaign understood something that many politicians were still learning: the Internet was not just a place to post press releases,” said one political analyst. “It was a place to build relationships, raise money, recruit volunteers, and make supporters feel like participants rather than spectators.”

## A Campaign Built for the Web

Obama’s 2008 campaign became famous for its digital sophistication. His team used email, text messages, online fundraising, and social networking platforms to mobilize millions of supporters. Small-dollar donations poured in through the campaign website, allowing Obama to compete financially with more established political figures.

Facebook played a particularly important role. Obama’s official Facebook page attracted millions of followers, giving the campaign a direct line to supporters across the country. The page was used to announce events, share videos, encourage voter registration, and amplify campaign messages.

“Facebook gave Obama a kind of political neighborhood,” said a technology strategist. “Supporters could gather there, share content, invite friends, and feel connected to a national movement. That was a major shift from traditional top-down campaigning.”

Unlike earlier campaigns that relied heavily on television advertising and direct mail, Obama’s team recognized that online supporters could become organizers in their own communities. A campaign message posted on Facebook could be shared thousands of times within minutes, reaching voters through trusted personal networks.

## YouTube and the New Presidential Address

After the election, Obama continued to experiment with digital communication. One of the most visible examples was his use of YouTube for weekly addresses. Presidents had long delivered weekly radio addresses, but Obama adapted the tradition for an online video audience.

By posting addresses on YouTube, Obama made presidential communication more accessible to younger voters and to citizens who increasingly consumed news online rather than through television or newspapers.

“Putting the weekly address on YouTube was symbolically important,” said a media scholar. “It showed that the Obama administration understood that the public square had moved. Americans were no longer waiting for information to come through three television networks. They were searching, sharing, and watching on demand.”

The YouTube addresses also allowed clips to circulate beyond their original audience. News outlets, bloggers, and ordinary citizens could embed or share the videos, extending their reach far beyond the White House website.

## Change.gov and the Digital Transition

Perhaps the clearest sign of Obama’s Internet-first approach came during the transition period, when his team launched Change.gov. The website was designed to provide information about the incoming administration, outline policy priorities, and invite citizens to submit ideas and personal stories.

Change.gov represented an effort to make the presidential transition more transparent and participatory. Visitors could learn about Obama’s agenda, apply for government jobs, and follow announcements from the transition team.

“Change.gov was an early attempt to turn campaign-style digital engagement into governing,” said a civic technology expert. “The message was: ‘We listened to you during the campaign, and we still want to hear from you now.’ That was a powerful idea, even if the practical limits of online participation became clear over time.”

The site reflected a broader promise of the Obama era: that technology could make government more open, responsive, and connected to citizens. While not every ambition was fully realized, the tone was unmistakably different from previous administrations.

## From Broadcast Politics to Networked Politics

Obama’s rise came at a moment when the Internet was reshaping American life. Facebook was expanding rapidly, YouTube had become a major video platform, and smartphones were beginning to transform how people consumed information. The Obama campaign met voters in these new digital spaces and helped normalize online political engagement.

Political observers noted that the campaign’s success was not simply about using new tools, but about understanding the culture of the Internet.

“Obama’s digital strategy worked because it matched the mood of the moment,” said a political communications expert. “It was participatory, fast-moving, visually compelling, and built around sharing. That made supporters feel like they were part of something larger than a conventional campaign.”

The approach also changed expectations for future candidates. After Obama, it became nearly impossible to run a serious national campaign without a sophisticated online strategy. Candidates were expected to maintain social media accounts, produce online video, raise money digitally, and respond quickly to online conversations.

## A Lasting Political Legacy

Obama was not the first president to use the Internet, but he was the first to make it central to his political identity. Bill Clinton’s White House launched an official website in the 1990s, and George W. Bush’s campaigns used online tools as well. But Obama’s 2008 campaign and early presidency represented a much deeper integration of digital media into modern politics.

His Facebook page helped turn supporters into online advocates. His YouTube addresses updated a presidential tradition for the digital era. Change.gov suggested that the tools of online organizing could be brought into the work of governing.

“Obama’s real innovation was not that he used the Internet,” said one analyst. “It was that he treated it as essential infrastructure for democracy in the 21st century.”

In the years since, digital politics has become more complicated. Social media has fueled activism and participation, but also misinformation, polarization, and distrust. Still, Obama’s 2008 campaign remains a landmark in the history of political communication.

By embracing Facebook, YouTube, and interactive websites, Barack Obama became the first president of the Internet age — a leader whose path to the White House showed that political power could now be built not only on rallies and television ads, but also on clicks, shares, streams, and online communities.

**Obama’s Digital Presidency: How the President-elect Plans to Bypass the Press and Speak Directly to Americans**

*By [Your Name], CNN Political Feature*

WASHINGTON — Barack Obama built the most technologically sophisticated campaign in presidential history. Now, as president-elect, he is preparing to bring that same digital machinery to the White House — potentially reshaping how presidents communicate with the public, mobilize supporters and pressure Congress.

After using e-mail lists, text messages, online video and social-networking sites to raise money and organize millions of voters, Obama’s team is exploring how to transform campaign tools into instruments of governance. The goal is clear: speak directly to Americans without relying solely on traditional media outlets to carry the message.

During the campaign, Obama’s online operation helped turn supporters into donors, volunteers and local organizers. Millions joined his social-media networks, signed up for e-mail updates or created accounts on My.BarackObama.com, the campaign’s organizing platform. That vast digital audience now represents something no incoming president has ever possessed at this scale: a ready-made national communications network.

For decades, presidents have depended on television networks, newspapers and the White House press corps to distribute their message. Obama is not abandoning those channels. But advisers see the Internet as a way to supplement — and at times bypass — the traditional filter.

Weekly radio addresses, for example, may be expanded into online video messages. Policy announcements could be posted directly to the Web. Supporters might receive e-mails asking them to call lawmakers, attend community meetings or build public support for legislation. Instead of waiting for the evening news, Americans could hear from the president through YouTube, Facebook, text alerts and the White House website.

That raises major questions about the future of **WhiteHouse.gov**. Historically, the site has served as a relatively static government portal, offering transcripts, biographies, statements and policy summaries. Under Obama, it could become a more dynamic hub — part information center, part organizing platform and part digital town hall.

Transition officials have already signaled an interest in greater transparency online. The Obama team has discussed posting more government information on the Web, using technology to solicit public feedback and making the White House’s digital presence more interactive. If the campaign model carries over, WhiteHouse.gov could feature videos, blogs, policy explainers, searchable documents and opportunities for citizens to participate more directly in the political process.

But governing is not campaigning. Once Obama takes office, his digital operation will face legal, ethical and practical constraints that did not apply to a campaign. Government resources cannot be used for partisan activity. Data collected by the campaign may not be freely merged with official White House communications. Messages from the president carry the weight of public office and must be handled differently than campaign appeals.

There is also the question of accountability. Traditional media outlets do more than transmit presidential messages; they question, investigate and challenge them. If the White House increasingly communicates directly with citizens, critics may worry that it is avoiding scrutiny. Supporters counter that online tools can make government more transparent, not less, by giving the public access to information without waiting for it to pass through political or media gatekeepers.

Obama’s success online has already changed expectations. His supporters are accustomed to immediate updates, personalized appeals and a sense of participation. Many will expect that relationship to continue after Inauguration Day. The challenge for the incoming administration will be turning campaign enthusiasm into civic engagement without treating citizens simply as members of a permanent political operation.

If Obama succeeds, the presidency could become more digitally connected than ever before. WhiteHouse.gov may evolve from a government brochure into a central platform for presidential communication. Social media could become a routine tool of executive leadership. And the millions of people who helped elect Obama online may become a powerful audience — and perhaps a political force — as he tries to govern.

The result could mark a turning point in presidential communication: from fireside chats, to televised addresses, to a White House that reaches Americans directly through the screens in their pockets and on their desks.
